text: Komodo dragons are the biggest lizards in the world. They use their forked tongues to smell the air.
A bearded dragon can puff out the spiky skin under its chin. It looks like a beard, and that is how it got its name.
Dragonflies have huge eyes. They can see in almost every direction at once.
A dragonfly can fly forward and backward. It can even stay still in one spot, like a tiny helicopter.
Leafy sea dragons are fish that look like floating seaweed. Their leafy fins help them hide in the ocean.
In a sea dragon family, the dad carries the eggs on the underside of his tail until they hatch.
Some small lizards called flying dragons can glide from tree to tree. They spread flaps of skin like wings.
A chameleon can move each eye on its own. It can look in two different ways at the same time.
Geckos can walk up walls and even across ceilings. Tiny hairs on their toes help them stick.

source.name: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Explorers: Gecko

text: Many lizards shed their old skin as they grow. A fresh new skin is waiting underneath.
Komodo dragons live on hot, rugged islands. They like to rest in the shade when the Sun gets too warm.
A bearded dragon can make its beard turn dark. A dark beard can mean it is alarmed or wants to look tough.
Dragonflies have four long wings. When they rest, most dragonflies hold their wings out flat, like an airplane.
The Komodo dragon lives on a few islands in Indonesia. It can grow to about ten feet long and is the largest lizard alive today.
Komodo dragons can hear, but not very well. Their forked tongue is their best tool, picking up smells from far away.
Bearded dragons come from the dry lands of Australia. They sometimes wave one front leg slowly, which scientists think is a signal to other bearded dragons.
Dragonflies begin life underwater as young insects. When they are ready, they climb up a plant stem and come out with wings.

source.name: Iowa DNR: 6 cool things about dragonflies

text: Dragonflies have four wings that can each move on their own. This lets them turn quickly, stop in midair, and even fly backward.

source.name: Iowa DNR: 6 cool things about dragonflies

text: Leafy sea dragons live only in the cool waters off southern and western Australia. They drift slowly and sway like seaweed, so few animals ever notice them.
Flying dragon lizards live in the forests of Southeast Asia. They open flaps of skin held out by long ribs and glide from one tree to another.
Chameleons change color to show how they feel and to warm up or cool down.
Geckos are among the few lizards that can make sounds. Some squeak, click, or bark softly to talk to each other.

source.name: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Explorers: Gecko

text: The marine iguana of the Galapagos Islands is the only lizard that swims in the sea to find its food. It munches on seaweed growing on underwater rocks.
The frilled lizard of Australia opens a big, colorful frill around its neck when it feels threatened. The frill helps keep other animals away.
The Chinese water dragon is a lizard that loves water. It is a strong swimmer and can stay underwater for many minutes by holding its breath.

source.name: Smithsonian National Zoo: Asian water dragon

text: A giraffe has a long, dark tongue. It uses its tongue to reach leaves high up in tall trees.
Elephants use their trunks to drink, to smell, to pick things up, and to greet their friends.
A hummingbird flaps its wings so fast that they make a humming sound. That is how it got its name.
Honeybees do a little dance to tell other bees where to find flowers full of food.
Penguins cannot fly, but they are great swimmers. Their wings work like flippers in the water.
An owl can turn its head about three quarters of the way around to look behind it.
Cats spend a big part of each day sleeping. Some cats sleep for more than half the day.

source.name: Britannica: Why do cats sleep so much

text: A baby kangaroo is called a joey. It rides in a warm pouch on its mother.
Butterflies can taste with their feet. A mother butterfly stands on a leaf to find out if it is a good plant for her eggs.
Sloths move so slowly that tiny green plants called algae can grow on their fur.

source.name: Smithsonian National Zoo: Why are sloths so slow

text: A snail carries its home on its back. When it feels unsafe, it pulls itself inside its shell.
Polar bears have black skin under their white fur. Thick fur and a layer of fat keep them warm in the snow.

source.name: Britannica: Why are polar bears white

text: Some parrots can learn to copy many words and sounds.
A group of flamingos is often called a flamboyance. Flamingos get their pink color from the tiny shrimp and algae they eat.

source.name: Smithsonian National Zoo: Why are flamingos pink

text: Arctic terns fly from the far north of the world to the far south and back again every year. That is one of the longest trips any animal makes.
Elephants make low rumbling sounds to talk to each other. Some of these sounds are so deep that people cannot hear them.
To make honey, honeybees must visit a very large number of flowers. They carry the sweet nectar back to the hive.
Owls can fly almost silently. Soft edges on their feathers help their wings stay quiet as they glide through the night.
Hummingbirds can hover in one spot and even fly backward. Their wings move in the shape of a figure eight.
A cheetah is the fastest land animal. In a short sprint, it can run about as fast as a car on a highway.
Some ants can carry things many times heavier than their own bodies. They often work as a team to move big loads.
Koalas spend most of the day asleep, often more than eighteen hours. The leaves they eat give them very little energy.
Each zebra has its own pattern of stripes, much like a fingerprint. No two zebras have exactly the same stripes.
Crows are very clever birds. They can remember the faces of people they have met.

source.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds: Remember me? Crows do

text: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs. It has a bill like a duck and finds its food underwater with its eyes closed.
The Sun is a star. It looks so big because it is much closer to us than any other star.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About the Sun

text: The Moon has no air and no wind. Footprints left by astronauts can stay there for a very long time.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About the Moon

text: Saturn has big, bright rings. They are made of chunks of ice and rock.
Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system. More than a thousand Earths could fit inside it.
Mars looks red because its dirt has rust in it. People call it the Red Planet.
Astronauts on the space station see the Sun rise and set many times every day.

source.name: NASA: Year in Space crew sunrises and sunsets

text: In space there is no air, so there is no sound. Astronauts use radios to talk to each other.

source.name: NASA Space Place: How Scary Is Space

text: The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight bounces off it.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About the Moon

text: Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick air holds in the heat like a blanket.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About Venus

text: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus, because the planet spins very slowly as it goes around the Sun.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About Venus

text: Scientists think there are more stars in space than grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth.

source.name: ESA: More stars than grains of sand on Earth

text: Shooting stars are not really stars. They are tiny bits of space rock glowing as they zip through the air.

source.name: NASA Science: Meteors and meteorites facts

text: The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth. It drifts a tiny bit farther each year.

source.name: NASA StarChild: Did you know the Moon

text: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the solar system. It is much taller than Mount Everest.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. When you see the Sun, you are seeing light that left it eight minutes ago.
Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system. They blow faster than the speed of sound on Earth.
Astronauts on the space station float because they are falling around the Earth all the time. They move so fast that they keep missing the ground.
Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in water, if there were a bathtub big enough to hold it.
Neptune is so far from the Sun that one trip around it takes about a hundred and sixty five Earth years.
A neutron star is so tightly packed that a single spoonful of it would weigh about as much as a mountain.

source.name: NASA Imagine the Universe: Neutron stars

text: The Milky Way is our home galaxy. On a dark night far from city lights, it looks like a faint, glowing band across the sky.

source.name: NASA Imagine the Universe: Milky Way

text: Mercury has almost no air to hold in heat. Its days are scorching hot, and its nights are freezing cold.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About Mercury

text: Jupiter has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot. The storm is wider than the whole Earth and has been swirling for hundreds of years.

source.name: NASA Science: Tour of storms across the solar system

text: A year on Mercury lasts only about three Earth months. It races around the Sun on the shortest path of any planet.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About Mercury

text: Mars has giant dust storms. Some grow so large that they wrap all the way around the planet.

source.name: NASA Science: Tour of storms across the solar system

text: Lava is melted rock. When it cools down, it turns hard and becomes new rock.

source.name: USGS: What is the difference between magma and lava?

text: Some volcanoes are under the sea. When they grow tall enough, they can make new islands.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration: How seamounts form

text: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain above the sea. It is so high that the air up there is thin and cold.
Diamonds are made of the same stuff as pencil lead. It is called carbon.
Some caves have stone shapes hanging from the ceiling like icicles. They grow drip by drip.

source.name: NOAA: Difference between a stalactite and a stalagmite

text: The center of the Earth is very hot. It is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Center of the Earth is as hot as the Sun

text: A rock called pumice is so full of tiny air holes that it can float on water.
A geyser is a hot spring that shoots water and steam high into the air.
Sand on many beaches is made of tiny bits of rock and shell, worn down by the waves.
Most of the Earth is covered by water. That is why it looks blue from space.
Salt is a crystal. If you look very closely, each grain of salt is a tiny cube.
Some lakes are so salty that people can float on top of the water with no effort.
Glaciers are huge rivers of ice. They move very, very slowly across the land.

source.name: NASA Climate Kids: 10 things about glaciers

text: Volcanic ash makes soil very rich. That is why farmers often grow crops on the slopes of old volcanoes.

source.name: British Geological Survey: Living with volcanoes

text: The islands of Hawaii were made by volcanoes rising from the sea floor. Some of those volcanoes are still adding new land today.
Obsidian is a shiny black glass made when lava cools very quickly. It cools so fast that crystals do not have time to form.
Mount Everest grows a tiny bit taller each year. Huge plates of rock under the ground slowly push together, and that helps lift it up.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Why Mount Everest grows taller each year

text: The Earth is made of layers, a bit like a peach. It has a thin crust, a thick mantle, and a metal core in the middle.
Geodes look like plain round rocks on the outside. When they are cracked open, many are lined with sparkling crystals.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth. A desert is any place that gets very little rain or snow, even if it is freezing cold.

source.name: Live Science: Largest desert on Earth

text: Quartz is one of the most common minerals in the crust of the Earth. Much of the sand on beaches is made of tiny grains of quartz.
Yellowstone National Park has about half of all the geysers in the world. Its most famous geyser, Old Faithful, erupts many times each day.

source.name: NPS Yellowstone: Old Faithful treasures, geysers

text: The Earth acts like a giant magnet. That is why the needle of a compass points north.
Iceland sits on a crack between two huge plates of rock. That is why it has so many volcanoes and hot springs.
Rubies and sapphires are the same mineral, called corundum. Tiny amounts of other metals make rubies red and sapphires blue.
A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through raindrops. The light splits into many colors.

source.name: Met Office: How are rainbows formed?

text: Most snowflakes have six sides or six arms. Each one is made of tiny ice crystals.
Clouds are made of tiny drops of water or bits of ice floating in the air.

source.name: NASA GPM: What are clouds made of?

text: A flash of lightning is hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Thunder is the sound that lightning makes. Light travels faster than sound, so we see the flash first.
Fog is a cloud that sits low, right down near the ground.
Hail is made of balls of ice that fall from big storm clouds.
Wind is moving air. The Sun warms some places more than others, and that makes the air move.
On cold nights, water in the air can freeze onto grass and windows. This sparkly ice is called frost.
On cool mornings, little drops of water called dew can appear on grass and spider webs.
Snow looks white because light bounces around in the ice and scatters back to your eyes.
A weather vane turns in the breeze. Its arrow points to where the wind is coming from.
Puddles dry up because the Sun warms the water. The water turns into a gas and floats into the air.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Evaporation and the water cycle

text: A cloud one cubic kilometer big holds water that weighs as much as about one hundred elephants. It floats because its drops are so tiny that rising air holds them up.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: How much does a cloud weigh

text: Scientists say it is very unlikely that two snowflakes are ever exactly alike. Each one takes its own path through the sky as it grows.

source.name: National Geographic: No two snowflakes the same

text: Raindrops are not really shaped like teardrops. Small ones are round, and bigger ones flatten out on the bottom like a bun as they fall.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Raindrops are different shapes

text: You can tell how far away a storm is by timing the seconds between lightning and thunder. Every five seconds is about one mile.
Rainbows are really full circles. From the ground we usually see only an arc, but people in airplanes can sometimes see the whole ring.
Mawsynram in India is one of the rainiest places on Earth. It gets more rain in a year than many cities get in ten years.
The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth. Some places there have gone years without any rain.

source.name: NASA Astrobiology: The driest place on Earth

text: Every day, weather balloons are sent up from hundreds of places around the world. They carry instruments high into the sky to measure the air.
A ring around the Moon is called a halo. It forms when moonlight passes through tiny ice crystals in thin, high clouds.

source.name: NWS La Crosse: Halos, sundogs and pillars

text: Sun dogs are bright spots of light that sometimes appear on each side of the Sun. Like halos, they are made by ice crystals in the sky.
Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth. Even in summer, much of it stays far below freezing.

source.name: NASA SVS: Coldest place on Earth

text: Lake effect snow happens when cold wind blows across a warmer lake. The wind picks up moisture and drops heavy snow on the land beyond it.

source.name: NOAA SciJinks: What is lake effect snow?

text: An octopus has three hearts. Its body is soft, with no bones at all.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Ten wild facts about octopuses

text: Sea otters sometimes hold paws while they sleep, so they do not drift away from their group.
The blue whale is the biggest animal on Earth. It can be about as long as a basketball court.
Starfish are not really fish, so scientists call them sea stars. Many of them have five arms.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Service: Sea star, not a fish

text: Seahorses swim standing up. They hold on to sea grass with their curly tails.
Clownfish live among the stinging arms of sea anemones. A special coat on their skin keeps them from getting stung.
Most of the ocean is very deep and dark. Some fish down there make their own light.
Dolphins rest one half of their brain at a time. That way they can keep swimming and breathing.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Dolphins sleep with half their brain

text: The ocean is salty because rivers carry tiny bits of salt from rocks into the sea.

source.name: WHOI: What makes the ocean salty?

text: Sea turtles can swim thousands of miles. Many females return to the beach where they were born to lay eggs.
Crabs walk sideways because of the way their legs bend.

source.name: UT Marine Science Institute: Why crabs scuttle sideways

text: Whales breathe air through blowholes on the top of their heads.
Sea stars have a tiny eye spot at the tip of each arm. The eye spots can tell light from dark.
The Pacific is the largest ocean. It is so big that all of the land on Earth could fit inside it.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Service: Largest ocean basin

text: The Great Barrier Reef off Australia is the largest structure on Earth built by living things. Astronauts can see it from space.

source.name: NASA Earth Observatory: Great Barrier Reef

text: The Mariana Trench is the deepest known part of the ocean. If Mount Everest were placed inside it, the peak would still be more than a mile under water.
An octopus can change both the color and the texture of its skin in a blink. This helps it blend in with rocks and coral.
Humpback whales sing long songs made of moans, cries, and squeaks. Their songs can travel for many miles through the water.

source.name: UT Marine Science Institute: The migration of whale songs

text: About half of the oxygen we breathe is made in the ocean, by tiny floating living things called plankton.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Service: How much oxygen comes from the ocean?

text: Coral may look like rock or plants, but each coral is made of many tiny animals called polyps.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration: Corals are animals

text: Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal. A single square inch of their fur can hold up to a million hairs.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Today: Sea otter anatomy

text: Most ocean waves are made by wind blowing across the water. The longer and harder the wind blows, the bigger the waves become.
The long tusk of a narwhal is really a tooth. It grows in a spiral and can be longer than a grown person is tall.
The longest mountain range on Earth is under the sea. It runs along the middle of the ocean floor, around the whole planet.
Emperor penguins dive deeper than any other bird. They can swim down more than a quarter of a mile to find food.

source.name: Australian Antarctic Division: Emperor penguin dive depth

text: Green sea turtles eat seaweed and sea grass. Scientists think this plant meal turns their body fat green, which gave them their name.

source.name: National Geographic Kids: Green sea turtle

text: Green sea turtles can swim more than a thousand miles across the open ocean. Scientists think they use the magnetic field of the Earth to find their way.

source.name: National Geographic Kids: Green sea turtle

text: A green sea turtle can rest underwater for several hours. When it is busy swimming, it comes up to breathe every few minutes.

source.name: National Geographic Kids: Green sea turtle

text: Flying snakes of Southeast Asia can glide through the air from tree to tree. They flatten their bodies to about twice their normal width.
A flying snake leaps from a branch and moves its body in a wavy S shape as it glides. It can even turn in midair to steer toward another tree.

source.name: Science News: Flying snakes glide through the treetops

text: Giant tortoises of the Galapagos Islands have two main shell shapes. Some have very round domed shells and live in cooler highlands. Others have saddleback shells that flare up at the front.

source.name: San Diego Zoo: Galapagos giant tortoise

text: An alligator has a wide, rounded snout. A crocodile has a narrower snout that looks more pointed.
Alligators mostly live in fresh water, such as swamps, marshes, rivers, and lakes. Many crocodiles can also live in salty water along coasts.
A dragonfly has five eyes. Its two large eyes are made of thousands of tiny lenses, and some kinds can even see ultraviolet light that people cannot see.
Some dragonflies can zoom along at more than twenty miles per hour. That makes them some of the fastest flying insects.
A young dragonfly lives underwater and sheds its skin six to fifteen times as it grows. After it climbs out as an adult, it takes several hours for its wings to fill and its body to harden.
Most of the life of a dragonfly is spent as a young insect in the water. It grows wings only at the very end.
Dragonflies can fly sideways as easily as forward. They can make sharp turns in the air faster than most other insects.
A red panda can munch about twenty thousand bamboo leaves in one day.
Red pandas can turn their ankles around so far that they climb down tree trunks headfirst. They also swing their long tails to stay balanced on branches.
A wombat digs long tunnels with its strong claws. The tunnels make a cozy home underground.
Wombats are marsupials, so a baby wombat grows up in a pouch on its mother. The pouch opens toward the back, which helps keep dirt out while she digs.
A beaver slaps its flat tail on the water to make a loud splash. It also uses the tail to help it swim.
Beavers have orange front teeth that never stop growing. They gnaw on wood, which keeps the teeth from getting too long.
A giant panda spends about twelve hours a day eating bamboo. It holds the stalks in its front paws.
Giant pandas have a special wrist bone that works a bit like a thumb. It helps them hold bamboo stalks tightly while they eat.
A river otter has webbed feet. They help it paddle and steer in the water.
River otters have a thick coat of fur that keeps water away from their skin. They spend lots of time swimming and sliding along muddy banks.
Camels have two rows of long eyelashes. They help keep sand out of their eyes in windy deserts.
A camel hump does not hold water. It stores fat, which the camel can use for energy when food is hard to find.

source.name: Britannica: Do camels store water in their humps

text: Gorillas build a new nest of leaves and branches to sleep in each night.
A gorilla troop is led by a strong, experienced male called a silverback. He decides where the troop travels and when it rests.
When a hedgehog feels unsafe, it curls into a tight ball. Its spiky coat then points in every direction.
A hedgehog has thousands of spines, which are really stiff hairs. It is most active at night, when it searches for food.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Their wings are thin skin stretched over long finger bones.
Most bats use sound to find their way in the dark. They make high squeaks and listen for the echoes that bounce back.
Bald eagles build huge nests of sticks high in trees. A pair may add to the same nest year after year.
A bald eagle has eyesight that is much sharper than ours. It can see things from up to a mile away while it soars high in the sky.
A woodpecker taps on trees with its strong beak. Stiff tail feathers help it hold on to the trunk.
Acorn woodpeckers store thousands of acorns in holes they drill in trees. Family groups share the work of looking after this food store.
An ostrich is the biggest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but it can run very fast on its long legs.
An ostrich has the biggest eyes of any bird, and its eggs are the largest of any bird. One egg weighs about as much as two dozen chicken eggs.
A male peafowl has a long train of colorful feathers. The train is covered in shiny spots that look like eyes.
Peafowl can fly short distances, even with long feathers. At night they often fly up to rest high in tall trees, where they feel safe.
A gray squirrel hides nuts in lots of spots. Sometimes it forgets where it put them.

source.name: Nat Geo Kids: Eastern Gray Squirrel

text: Squirrels use their bushy tails for balance when they leap from branch to branch, a bit like a tightrope walker uses a long pole.

source.name: University of Notre Dame: Springing Squirrels

text: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system. It is only a little more than one third as wide as the Earth.
Mercury has no moons and no rings. It is the closest planet to the Sun, and it is only a little bigger than our Moon.
One full day and night on Mercury, from one sunrise to the next, lasts about a hundred and seventy six Earth days. That is twice as long as a year on Mercury.
Venus spins the opposite way from most planets. If you could stand there, the Sun would rise in the west.
Only the Sun and the Moon look brighter in our sky than Venus. Many people mistake it for a very bright star.
Venus is almost the same size as the Earth, about ninety five percent as wide. Thick clouds cover the whole planet, and winds at the cloud tops blow faster than two hundred miles an hour.
Almost all of the water on our planet is salty ocean water. Only a small part is fresh water that we can drink.
The air around the Earth is mostly nitrogen. Only about one part in five is the oxygen that we breathe.
The Earth is about ninety three million miles from the Sun. Scientists call this distance one astronomical unit and use it like a ruler to measure space.
Mars has two small moons. Their names are Phobos and Deimos.
A day on Mars lasts about twenty four and a half hours. That is very close to a day on the Earth.
Valles Marineris is a giant canyon on Mars, about twenty four hundred miles long. It is the largest canyon in the solar system.
Sunlight takes about thirteen minutes to reach Mars, because Mars is much farther from the Sun than the Earth is.
A day on Jupiter lasts less than ten hours. It spins faster than any other planet in the solar system.
Jupiter has faint rings made of tiny, dark bits. A spacecraft called Voyager one found them.
In sixteen ten, Galileo Galilei spotted four moons circling Jupiter. They are named Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Ganymede is a moon of Jupiter, and it is the biggest moon in the solar system. It is even bigger than the planet Mercury.
Saturn has wide rings, but they are very thin. In many places they are only about thirty feet thick.
Near the north pole of Saturn, a strong river of wind blows in the shape of a six sided hexagon. The shape is about twenty thousand miles across.
A moon of Saturn has lakes of liquid methane, and another moon, Enceladus, shoots out jets of water. Scientists think both moons may have oceans hidden inside.
Neptune was found with math. An astronomer used odd wobbles in the path of another planet to predict where to look, and the planet was spotted in eighteen forty six.
Neptune looks blue. A gas called methane in its air soaks up other colors, so more blue light bounces back to us.
Voyager two was the first spacecraft to fly past Neptune. It made the trip in the summer of nineteen eighty nine.
Triton, the biggest moon of Neptune, circles the planet in the opposite direction to the way Neptune spins. It was found just seventeen days after the planet itself.
The Sun is about a hundred times wider than the Earth. More than a million Earths could fit inside it.
Almost all of the stuff in our solar system is in the Sun. All the planets together are only a tiny part.
The center of the Sun is about fifteen million degrees Celsius. That is hot enough for the nuclear fusion that keeps the Sun shining.
Sunspots are dark patches on the surface of the Sun. Some are far wider than the whole Earth.
The Sun spins, but not like a solid ball. It takes about twenty five Earth days to turn at its middle and about thirty six days near its poles.
After the Sun, the closest star to us is Proxima Centauri. Its light takes about four years to reach the Earth.
We always see the same side of the Moon. It turns just once each time it goes around the Earth.
Gravity on the Moon is only one sixth as strong as on the Earth. That is why astronauts seemed to bounce when they walked.
Apollo astronauts brought back more than eight hundred pounds of Moon rock and dust for scientists to study.
Tycho is a crater on the Moon that is more than fifty miles wide. Craters last a very long time there, because there is no wind or rain to wear them away.
The dark patches you can see on the Moon are called maria, a word that means seas. They are not water. They are flat plains filled with hardened lava.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About the Moon

text: The first people landed on the Moon in July of nineteen sixty nine, during a mission called Apollo eleven.

source.name: NASA Space Place: All About the Moon

text: Hubble is a telescope that flies around the Earth. It was sent into space in nineteen ninety.
The Hubble telescope has helped scientists learn what the air is made of on planets that circle other stars.
The Webb telescope has a giant mirror covered with a thin layer of gold. It was built to look at the sky in infrared light.
The Webb telescope folded up like origami to fit inside a rocket, then opened out in space. Its sunshield has five layers to block heat from the Sun, Earth and Moon.
Each Voyager spacecraft carries a Golden Record filled with sounds and pictures from the Earth. A team led by Carl Sagan chose what to put on it.
Voyager one turned its camera back and took a picture of the Earth from about three point seven billion miles away. The Earth looked like a tiny speck of dust in a sunbeam.
Voyager one and Voyager two both flew out past the bubble of particles and magnetic fields around the Sun, into the space between the stars.
The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth. Its huge basin drains a vast part of South America.
The Amazon River is about four thousand miles long. That makes it one of the longest rivers on the planet.
Lake Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth. At its deepest point it is more than a mile from top to bottom.
Lake Baikal holds about one fifth of all the liquid fresh water found on the surface of the Earth. No other lake holds more.
A kind of seal lives only in Lake Baikal. It swims in fresh water, not in the salty sea.
Lake Baikal freezes over in winter. The ice stays from about January until May or June.
The Sahara fills most of northern Africa and covers more than three million square miles. It is the biggest hot desert on Earth.
Sand dunes cover only about one quarter of the Sahara. Most of this big desert is not sandy at all.
People in the Sahara grow date palms at oases. An oasis is a spot where water can be found in the desert.
Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is the tallest mountain in Africa. It is about nineteen thousand feet high.
Mount Kilimanjaro stands alone instead of being part of a mountain range. It is made of three volcanic cones named Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.
The Giants Causeway in Northern Ireland has about forty thousand stone columns. Most of them have six sides, like a honeycomb.
The stone columns of the Giants Causeway formed when a flow of lava cooled and shrank. As it shrank, the rock cracked into tall columns.
Steamboat Geyser in Yellowstone is the tallest active geyser in the world. Its water can shoot three hundred to four hundred feet into the air.
A geyser has a narrow place in its underground pipes that traps hot water. When steam bubbles push the water upward, the geyser bursts out.
The General Sherman Tree is a giant sequoia in Sequoia National Park. Its trunk is about thirty six feet wide at the bottom.
The General Sherman Tree weighs nearly fourteen hundred tons. That is a lot of wood for a single tree.
The National Park Service takes care of more than four thousand caves. Some of them stretch for more than a hundred miles underground.
The Great Barrier Reef is more than a thousand miles long. It is made of thousands of smaller reefs and many islands.
High clouds float more than three miles above the ground. Low clouds stay below about a mile and a quarter.
Cirrus clouds are made mostly of ice crystals. The wind stretches the crystals into thin, wispy strands.
Some clouds look like rows of little puffs. They are made of tiny drops of liquid water and hardly ever bring rain.
Stratus clouds spread out in flat gray layers and seldom bring much rain or snow. On hills and mountains, they can look like fog.
Jets high in the sky leave long white trails called contrails. These trails are clouds made from water vapor in the engine air.
Huge storm clouds grow on hot days, when warm, wet air rises very high. From far away, they look like giant towers or mountains in the sky.
Puffy white clouds look like balls of cotton. They often float in the sky on sunny days.
Most of the water in the sky is an invisible gas called water vapor. When the air cools, the vapor turns into drops that gather around specks of dust, ice or sea salt.
Rain starts when tiny cloud drops join together. Once the drops grow heavy enough, gravity pulls them down to the ground.
At night, clouds work like a blanket and keep the ground warmer. In the day, they give us shade.
Clouds are not only on Earth. Jupiter has clouds made of a gas called ammonia.
When the air is cold enough, clouds can make snow, sleet or freezing rain instead of plain rain.
Mars has clouds that look a lot like the clouds on Earth.
Scientists use satellites to study clouds from space. The pictures help them learn about the weather on Earth.
Yearly rainfall can be less than a tenth of an inch in some deserts. In the rainiest parts of the tropics, it can be more than four hundred inches.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Rain and precipitation

text: Mount Waialeale, in Hawaii, gets hundreds of inches of rain in an average year. It is one of the rainiest places in the United States.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Rain and precipitation

text: In the year eighteen sixty one, the town of Cherrapunji in India measured about nine hundred inches of rain in a single year.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Rain and precipitation

text: One inch of rain falling on a single acre of ground is about twenty seven thousand gallons of water. That much water weighs more than a hundred tons.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Rain and precipitation

text: A common rule says ten inches of snow melts into about one inch of water. Wet, heavy snow holds more water, and light, fluffy snow holds less.

source.name: USGS Water Science School: Rain and precipitation

text: The tiny gas molecules in the air scatter blue light much more than red light. That scattering is why the daytime sky looks blue.

source.name: Met Office: Why the sky is blue and sunsets red

text: Violet light scatters even more than blue light. But sunlight has less violet, and our eyes see blue better, so the sky looks blue instead of purple.

source.name: Met Office: Why the sky is blue and sunsets red

text: The sky looks paler near the horizon than it does straight overhead. The light has to cross much more air to reach you.

source.name: Met Office: Why the sky is blue and sunsets red

text: At sunset, the Sun is low, so its light crosses a thick layer of air. The blue light gets scattered away, and the red and orange light is left.

source.name: Met Office: Why the sky is blue and sunsets red

text: Space looks black because it has almost no air. With no air molecules, there is nothing to scatter the sunlight.

source.name: NWS Flagstaff: Why is the sky blue

text: High up on a mountain, there are fewer air molecules overhead. The sky there can look a deeper blue, or even a bluish violet.

source.name: NWS Flagstaff: Why is the sky blue

text: Violet has the shortest wavelength of the colors we can see, and red has the longest. That difference decides how much each color is scattered by the air.

source.name: NWS Flagstaff: Why is the sky blue

text: Extra bits in the air, such as dust, can make a sunrise or a sunset look more colorful.

source.name: NWS Flagstaff: Why is the sky blue

text: The Earth is closest to the Sun in January and farthest from it in July. The gap is only about three million miles, so distance does not cause the seasons.

source.name: NASA Space Place: What causes the seasons

text: The axis of the Earth leans about twenty three degrees. It points the same way all year long while the Earth travels around the Sun, and that tilt makes the seasons.

source.name: NOAA NESDIS: Why does Earth have seasons

text: Around June, the North Pole leans toward the Sun. That gives the north half of the world its summer.

source.name: NASA Space Place: What causes the seasons

text: When it is summer in the north half of the world, it is winter in the south half. The seasons are opposite.

source.name: NOAA NESDIS: Why does Earth have seasons

text: In the north half of the world, the winter Sun rises in the southeast and sets in the southwest. In summer, the Sun climbs much higher and passes more directly overhead.

source.name: NOAA NESDIS: Why does Earth have seasons

text: The Earth spins around once each day. That spin gives us day and night.

source.name: NASA Space Place: What causes the seasons

text: To see a rainbow, you need the Sun behind you and raindrops in front of you. The light bends and bounces inside each drop.
When the Sun is high, you see only a small rainbow arc near the ground. A lower Sun gives a taller arc.
Isaac Newton made the idea of seven rainbow colors popular. In truth, a rainbow has a smooth range of colors that blend into each other.
Moonlight can make a rainbow too, called a moonbow. It usually looks white to our eyes and needs a bright, nearly full Moon.
A double rainbow has a fainter bow on the outside with its colors in reverse order. The light bounces twice inside the raindrops to make it.
Light leaves the raindrops that make a rainbow at an angle of about forty two degrees. That is why the Sun must be lower than forty two degrees in the sky.
In the main bow of a rainbow, red is on the outside edge and violet is along the inside edge.
Auroras come from space weather. Charged particles from the Sun reach the Earth and meet its magnetic field, which makes the sky glow.
Auroras are mostly green. They can also have hints of yellow, pink, purple and white.
People see auroras most often in far northern places like Canada, Greenland and Alaska.
Auroras can be photographed from space. Astronauts on the International Space Station and satellites have both taken pictures of them.
An octopus has eight arms. A squid has eight arms and two extra long ones called tentacles.
Squid, cuttlefish, and octopuses use a molecule with copper in it to carry oxygen around the body. This molecule makes their blood blue.
Some octopuses can open jars to get what is inside. Scientists think they are very smart and good at solving puzzles.
A squid pulls water into its body and shoots it out of a funnel. The water goes one way and the squid goes the other, like a tiny jet.
The nautilus has a shell with chambers full of gas. It can float up or down, a bit like a submarine.
The giant squid is the longest cephalopod in the world. Scientists think the biggest ones can reach about forty feet from end to end.
A pygmy squid is so small that it could sit on the tip of your finger.
A big California sea lion can grow as long as eight feet and weigh up to one thousand pounds.

source.name: National Geographic Kids: California sea lion

text: California sea lions can dive down to about nine hundred feet. They can hold their breath for nearly ten minutes by slowing down their heartbeat.

source.name: National Geographic Kids: California sea lion

text: There are five named oceans on Earth. They all join together, so they really make one big world ocean.
The five oceans are the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern, and the Arctic. Together they make one huge body of salt water.
The ocean is very deep. On average, it is a little more than two miles from the top to the bottom.
Scientists think there may be as many as seven hundred thousand kinds of sea life, and most of them have not been named yet.
About ninety five percent of sea animals are invertebrates, which means they have no backbone. Crabs, jellyfish, and octopuses are all invertebrates.
Some giant manta rays have wings that stretch twenty feet from tip to tip. That is wider than most cars are long.
Scientists say most of the deep ocean has never been seen by people. That leaves a huge amount still to discover.
Temperature, depth, and distance from shore all decide which plants and animals can live in a part of the ocean.
One study by ocean scientists found that about three quarters of the animals in the deep sea make their own light.
Most light made by ocean animals is blue green, probably because those colors travel the farthest through sea water.
Hatchetfish have rows of tiny lights on their bellies. The glow matches the light shining down from above.
A lanternfish has tiny lights along its belly. Some also have a light by the nose that works like a headlight.
The Moon has about twice as much effect on our ocean tides as the Sun does, because the Moon is so much closer to the Earth.
The Earth has two tidal bulges of water at once, one on each side. That is why high tides happen on opposite sides of the planet at the same time.
Spring tides have nothing to do with the season. They happen when the Sun and Moon line up. That brings very high highs and very low lows.
Neap tides are the gentlest tides. They happen when the Sun and Moon sit at a right angle to each other as seen from the Earth.
Tides are the slow rise and fall of the sea. The Moon helps pull the water up.
Coral can grow on old ships that were sunk on purpose to make new homes for fish. Over time, the ships turn into reefs.
An atoll is a ring of coral reef with a calm lagoon in the middle. It builds up slowly over many years around an island.
Corals, sponges, and algae are the main parts of most coral reefs. Colorful fish swim all around them.
Tiny algae live inside coral polyps. The algae and the polyps share a partnership that helps them both.
A manatee can grow about fifteen feet long. It eats only plants.
Manatees breathe air with lungs, so they swim up to the surface for breaths. Their flat, round tails push them forward through the water.
A baby manatee is called a calf. It stays close to its mother for up to two years.
There are three kinds of manatee. One lives near the Amazon River, one near West Africa, and one around Florida and the West Indies.
Most seals can stay under water for twenty to thirty minutes. Weddell seals can stay down for more than an hour.
Elephant seals are the biggest seals. They can be longer than twenty feet and weigh more than eight thousand pounds.
Seven spotted ladybugs are red or orange. They have three spots on each side and one spot in the middle.
There are about five thousand kinds of ladybugs around the world. Gardeners and farmers are happy to see them because they help keep plants healthy.
Fireflies are not flies at all. They are a kind of beetle that can light up in the dark.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: 14 fun facts about fireflies

text: Many kinds of fireflies have their own special pattern of flashes. Their light can be yellow, green, or orange.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: 14 fun facts about fireflies

text: Monarch butterflies have orange wings with black lines and white dots along the edges. Their wings are about as wide as your hand.
Some monarch butterflies fly up to three thousand miles to reach warmer places for the winter. They cannot live through freezing weather, so they travel south before it gets cold.
A honeybee hive usually has just one queen. She lays the eggs that become the next bees.
Worker honeybees have many jobs. They gather pollen and nectar, build and clean the hive, and fan air through it with their wings.
Ants have bent antennae that look like tiny elbows. The antennae help them sense the world around them.
Scientists know of more than twelve thousand kinds of ants. Some build nests underground, some build mounds above the ground, and some live in trees.
Crickets chirp by rubbing their front wings together. Warmer weather makes them chirp faster.
A frog starts as an egg. The egg hatches into a tadpole with a long tail and gills, just like a fish.
Frogs can breathe through their moist skin as well as with their lungs. Their large, bulging eyes let them see in almost every direction.

source.name: San Diego Zoo: Frog and Toad

text: Toads usually have drier, bumpy skin and shorter legs. Frogs usually have smooth, moist skin, longer legs, and a home close to water.

source.name: San Diego Zoo: Frog and Toad

text: An axolotl is a salamander with feathery gills that stick out behind its head. It lives in the water its whole life.
Most salamanders change a lot as they grow up, but an axolotl keeps its baby features even as an adult. That is why it keeps its feathery gills all its life.
A spotted salamander is bluish black with bright yellow or orange spots. It is about seven inches long.
Spotted salamanders stay hidden under rocks, leaves, and logs during the day. They come out at night, and their young live in the water until they lose their gills.
A dog has a super nose. Its sense of smell is many thousands of times better than ours.
Some dogs have important jobs, such as guiding people who cannot see or helping rescue teams search for lost people. There are several hundred kinds of dogs, and they all belong to one species.
A cat uses its whiskers to feel the world around it. Whiskers are tiny sense organs that are made for touch.
Cat claws stay tucked away most of the time, which keeps them sharp. Cats can see much better in dim light than people can, but not in total darkness.
A rabbit has strong front teeth that never stop growing. They are shaped like little chisels.
Each ear of a rabbit can move on its own to catch sounds from different directions. Its eyes sit on the sides of its head, so it can see in nearly every direction.
Hamsters have big cheek pouches for carrying food. They are most active in the evening and at night.
Wild hamsters dig burrows with separate rooms for sleeping and for storing food. Adult golden hamsters, the kind many people keep as pets, are only about five or six inches long.
A baby horse is called a foal. It can stand up soon after it is born.
Horses can doze while standing because special tendons and ligaments lock the joints in their legs. Adult horses sleep only a few hours each day.
Some kinds of cows, such as Jersey and Holstein cows, are raised mainly for their milk. Milk can be made into cheese and butter.
Highland cattle have long, shaggy hair, while Brahman cattle have loose skin and long, drooping ears. There are many breeds of cattle, and they differ in color and size.
A pig has a leathery snout that is very sensitive to touch. It uses its snout to root around in the ground.
Pigs roll in mud to cool off, but they are actually quite clean animals. They are also among the smartest farm animals.
Most farm sheep grow a thick coat called wool. People use wool to make cloth.
Both male and female goats can have horns. Most male goats also grow beards.
Wild goats can scramble up steep cliffs and rocks without slipping. People drink the milk of farm goats and use it to make cheese.
Both hens and roosters have a comb. It is a bit of skin that sticks up from the top of the head.
A hen can lay more than two hundred eggs in a year. Chickens have short wings and heavy bodies, so they cannot fly very far.
The Grand Canyon is about a mile deep in places. Its rock walls show many colorful layers.
The Grand Canyon is about two hundred seventy seven miles long and up to about eighteen miles wide. The Colorado River flows along the bottom.
The North Rim of the Grand Canyon is about a thousand feet higher than the South Rim. The rims are only about ten miles apart in a straight line, but hiking between them takes about twenty one miles.
Niagara Falls is really three waterfalls side by side. The biggest one is shaped like a horseshoe.
During summer days, more than one hundred fifty thousand cubic meters of water rush over Niagara Falls every minute. Most of that water goes over the big Horseshoe Falls.
Niagara Falls is very loud and misty. Visitors can ride boats close to the bottom of the falls and feel the cool spray on their faces.
The Niagara River flows from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario, and the falls sit between New York and Ontario. Big power plants nearby use the moving water to make electricity.
Uluru is more than two miles long and more than a mile wide. It sits in a national park near the middle of Australia.
Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system in the world. It has more than four hundred miles of mapped passages.
Deep inside Mammoth Cave, the air stays cool all year, at about fifty four degrees Fahrenheit.
Mammoth Cave formed as water slowly dissolved limestone. That kind of rock is soft enough for water to wear away, and the work is still going on today.
Some stone shapes in Mammoth Cave have fun names, such as Frozen Niagara.
Talc is the softest mineral. It is so soft that a fingernail can scratch it. Diamond is the hardest.
Many people think only diamonds can scratch glass. In fact, many other minerals that rank six or higher on the Mohs scale can scratch it too.
A copper coin can scratch some very soft minerals, such as talc and gypsum.
Rocks come in three main kinds. Igneous rocks form when melted rock cools, sedimentary rocks form from pressed layers, and metamorphic rocks are changed by heat and pressure.
Granite forms when melted rock cools slowly underground. Basalt forms when lava cools at the surface.
Sandstone and shale are rocks made of tiny bits pressed together in layers.
Slate and gneiss are rocks that were changed by heat and pressure underground. Gneiss is said like the word nice.
Mount Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan, at about twelve thousand four hundred feet. It is a snowcapped cone with a nearly perfect shape, and artists love to paint it.
Five small lakes sit at the northern base of Mount Fuji. On calm days, Lake Kawaguchi shows the mountain in its water like a mirror.
Greenland is the biggest island in the world. Ice covers most of it.
The ice sheet on Greenland is almost two miles thick in places. Only the ice sheet of Antarctica is bigger.
Parts of Greenland get midnight sun, with daylight all night long, for weeks in summer. In the long, dark winter, the sky there often fills with bright colors.
Measured from its base on the sea floor, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is about thirty three thousand feet tall. That is taller than Mount Everest.
An emerald is a deep green gem. Tiny amounts of metals such as chromium give it its color.
Emerald scores about seven and a half to eight on the Mohs scale, while diamond scores ten. Tiny cracks inside many emeralds mean that they can chip easily.
In a cave in Mexico, giant crystals of selenite, a form of gypsum, fill a huge underground room. Some of the crystals are about thirty seven feet long.
A gold nugget is a lump of gold that water has worn smooth. Many are as small as a pea or a nut.
Great Salt Lake in Utah is usually three to five times saltier than the ocean. Fish cannot live in it, but tiny brine shrimp do, and many birds stop there on long trips.
The space station moves at about seventeen thousand five hundred miles an hour. It circles the Earth about once every ninety minutes.
Astronauts sleep in sleeping bags that are strapped to a wall. They also use a sleep mask and earplugs to block out light and noise.

source.name: NASA Living and Working in Space fact sheet

text: The living space inside the space station is about as big as a house with six bedrooms. With its solar panels spread out, the whole station is as wide as a football field.
Astronauts on the space station exercise for about two hours every day. It keeps their muscles and bones strong.

source.name: NASA Living and Working in Space fact sheet

text: A spacesuit is like a tiny spacecraft that you wear. It gives an astronaut air to breathe and water to drink.

source.name: NASA: What Is a Spacesuit? (grades K to 4)

text: The visor on a spacesuit helmet has a thin gold coating. It shields the eyes of the astronaut from bright sunlight.

source.name: NASA: What Is a Spacesuit? (grades K to 4)

text: Under a spacesuit, astronauts wear a special layer with thin tubes in it. Cool water flows through the tubes to keep the astronaut from getting too hot.

source.name: NASA: What Is a Spacesuit? (grades K to 4)

text: The backpack of a spacesuit stores oxygen, removes the carbon dioxide that an astronaut breathes out, and supplies electricity. A fan and a water tank are inside it too.

source.name: NASA: What Is a Spacesuit? (grades K to 4)

text: A spacesuit is made of many layers. Each layer does a different job, like keeping the air inside the suit.

source.name: NASA: What Is a Spacesuit? (grades K to 4)

text: A comet is a ball of ice, rock and dust. When it gets close to the Sun, it warms up and grows a long tail.

source.name: NASA Space Place: Comet Fun Sheet

text: A comet can have more than one tail. Its gas tail points straight away from the Sun, while its dust tail curves along the path of the comet.

source.name: NASA Space Place: Comet Fun Sheet

text: When a comet warms up near the Sun, a cloud called the coma forms around its solid center. The cloud can be hundreds of thousands of miles across.

source.name: NASA Space Place: Comet Fun Sheet

text: The solid center of a comet is usually less than about six miles across. Its glowing cloud can be much bigger.

source.name: NASA Space Place: Comet Fun Sheet

text: Comet Halley comes back to our part of the sky about every seventy six years. It is next expected in the year twenty sixty one.
Dust left behind by Comet Halley makes two meteor showers each year. One comes in May and the other in October.
About once a year, a comet comes close enough and grows bright enough to be seen without a telescope.

source.name: NASA Space Place: Comet Fun Sheet

text: The Big Dipper is a group of stars that looks like a big ladle for dipping soup.
Astronomers divide the sky into eighty eight official star patterns. They use them like landmarks to find stars and to name stars and meteor showers.
The stars in a star pattern may look close together, but they are not connected. They can be at very different distances from the Earth.
Which star patterns you can see depends on where you live and on the time of year, because the Earth travels around the Sun.
Stars are still in the sky during the day. The bright light of the Sun hides them.
Sailors have long used the stars to find their way across the sea. Robot spacecraft also compare star patterns to maps of the sky to know where they are pointing.
Blue stars are hotter than red stars. The color of a star is a clue to how hot it is.

source.name: NASA Imagine the Universe: star colors activity

text: Apollo eleven had three astronauts. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon, while Michael Collins circled above them.
The lunar module of Apollo eleven was named Eagle. It landed on a flat plain called the Sea of Tranquility.
The Apollo eleven astronauts spent more than twenty one hours on the Moon. Only about two and a half hours of that time was spent walking on the surface.
A plaque on the leg of the Apollo eleven lunar module showed a map of the Earth. It said that men from Earth came in peace for all mankind.
Apollo eleven astronauts left a seismometer on the Moon to measure moonquakes. They also set up a reflector that bounces laser beams back to the Earth.
The whole Apollo eleven trip to the Moon and back took about eight days.
A green iguana uses its strong tail to swim. It can hold its breath underwater for up to thirty minutes.
Adult green iguanas eat mostly fruits, flowers, and leaves. A grown male can reach a length of about four to six and a half feet.
Basilisk lizards can run across the top of the water on their back legs. After about fifteen feet, they sink down and swim.

source.name: National Geographic: basilisks walk on water

text: Each step of a basilisk lizard slaps the water and makes a small pocket of air around its foot. That air pocket holds the lizard up for a moment while it runs.

source.name: National Geographic: basilisks walk on water

text: Horned lizards have wide, flat bodies with spiky skin. They look a bit like tiny toads, but they are really lizards.

source.name: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Horned lizard facts

text: Texas horned lizards are only about three and a half to five inches long. Their gray, brown, and rust colors help them blend in with the plants and dry ground around them.

source.name: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Horned lizard facts

text: The leatherback is the biggest sea turtle. It has no hard shell, and its back is covered with firm, rubbery skin.
Leatherback sea turtles nest in warm places such as Florida and Puerto Rico, yet they swim as far north as the waters off Canada.
A green anole has a pink or red flap of skin under its chin called a dewlap. It shows the flap off to others.
A green anole is not always green. It can change its color from bright green to brown, and back again.

source.name: Kennesaw State University: Green anole color change

text: Galapagos giant tortoises are among the largest tortoises alive today. A big one can be about five feet long.

source.name: San Diego Zoo library: Galapagos tortoises fact sheet

text: Giant tortoises munch on grass, shrubs, and prickly pear cactus. Their long necks help them reach the plants.

source.name: San Diego Zoo library: Galapagos tortoises fact sheet

text: The top of a turtle shell is called the carapace, and the bottom is called the plastron. The two parts usually join along the sides to make a strong box around the body.
A box turtle has a hinge on the bottom of its shell. It can pull in its head and legs and shut its shell almost completely.

source.name: Smithsonian National Zoo: Eastern box turtle

text: An eastern box turtle has a dark brown shell with bright orange and yellow marks. Those colors help it blend in with the leaves and damp soil of the forest floor.

source.name: Smithsonian National Zoo: Eastern box turtle

text: The eastern blue tongue lizard has a bright blue tongue. It sticks the tongue out to show it off against its pink mouth.

source.name: Australian Museum: Eastern blue tongue lizard

text: A ball python curls up in a tight ball when it feels nervous. That is how it got its name.
Ball pythons live in central and western Africa, along the edges of forests. They grow to about three to five feet long, which is smaller than most of the large snakes.
Garter snakes often have a thin yellow stripe down the back. They are good swimmers, and some can climb into low bushes.
A corn snake is orange with red blotches outlined in black. Its belly has a black and white check pattern.
Corn snakes live in the woods, meadows, and rocky hillsides of the eastern United States. They are shy, so they like to climb trees or hide under logs and rocks.
A weedy seadragon has a long, pipe shaped snout with a tiny mouth at the end. It is a cousin of the seahorse.
Weedy seadragons are red and yellow with tiny purple and blue marks. Small leafy flaps on their bodies look like bits of seaweed, which helps them hide among the real seaweed.
There are about twenty five hundred kinds of dragonflies. They live near ponds, lakes, and streams in most parts of the world.
Kelp is a big brown seaweed that grows in cool water. It can grow about a foot and a half in one day.
Kelp forests need sunlight, so they grow in fairly shallow water. Seals, sea lions, otters, and birds such as gulls and herons all visit these underwater forests for food or shelter.
A fish called the cabezon lives on the rocky bottom of kelp forests. It guards its brightly colored eggs.

source.name: NOAA Sanctuaries: Monterey Bay living gallery

text: People have looked closely at only a tiny part of the deep sea floor. Most of the deep ocean is still waiting to be explored, and scientists still find new animals there.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration: How much of the ocean has been explored?

text: Satellites have mapped the whole sea floor, but only in a blurry way. Ships that use sonar make much sharper maps, and so far they have mapped only part of it.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration: How much of the ocean has been explored?

text: An ROV is a robot that explores under the sea. Some are as small as a laptop, and some are as big as a small truck.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration: ROV fact sheet

text: A tether of cables links an ROV to its ship and brings it power. The ROV has bright lights, several cameras, and a robot arm that can pick up samples for scientists to study.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Exploration: ROV fact sheet

text: In nineteen sixty, two men rode a deep diving craft called the Trieste to the bottom of the Challenger Deep. They stayed on the bottom for about twenty minutes.
Seashells are made by soft bodied animals called mollusks, such as snails and clams. The hard shell gives their soft bodies support and protection.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: The story behind the seashells by the seashore

text: Many seashells are made of calcium carbonate, the same mineral found in eggshells. The animal makes its shell bigger by adding new material along the edge.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: The story behind the seashells by the seashore

text: A hermit crab does not make a shell of its own. It finds an empty shell and uses it as a home.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: The story behind the seashells by the seashore

text: Some beaches in Hawaii and Iceland have black sand. It forms when hot lava meets the sea and breaks into dark grains.

source.name: Ocean Conservancy: Top facts about the beach

text: Some beaches in Bermuda and the Bahamas have pink sand. Tiny sea creatures called foraminifera leave behind pink shells, and these mix with crushed coral.

source.name: Ocean Conservancy: Top facts about the beach

text: A puffin flaps its wings up to four hundred times a minute. Under water, it uses its wings like paddles to swim.
Puffins dig burrows with their beaks and claws, often between big rocks. They line the burrow with feathers and grass, and many pairs use the same one again year after year.
A Laysan albatross can spread its wings more than six feet wide. It glides over the open ocean.
Arctic terns spend summer in the far north and then fly south to enjoy another summer near Antarctica. The round trip is more than twenty five thousand miles each year.

source.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds: Arctic Tern

text: Arctic terns nest on the ground in big groups called colonies. They can live for decades.

source.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds: Arctic Tern

text: The ocean sunfish is among the heaviest bony fish in the world. It can weigh as much as five thousand pounds.

source.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Unraveling the mysteries of the ocean sunfish

text: An ocean sunfish has a flat, round body and no true tail. It often rests near the surface, as if it were soaking up the sunshine.
The top of a wave is called the crest, and the low spot between waves is the trough. The distance from one crest to the next is the wavelength.

source.name: Smithsonian Ocean: The anatomy of a wave

text: A wave carries energy across the sea. The water itself does not travel very far.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Today: Why does the ocean have waves?

text: A tide station in San Francisco has been measuring the height of the sea for more than a hundred and fifty years. Tides are caused by the pull of the Moon and the Sun.

source.name: NOAA Ocean Service: Tides and tidal waves

text: A windsock is a cloth tube that shows which way the wind blows. It droops in light wind and stands out straight in strong wind.
Airports use windsocks so pilots can check the wind. When a windsock stands straight out, the wind is blowing at about seventeen miles per hour or more.
A barometer is a tool that measures air pressure. People use it to help guess what the weather will do next.

source.name: Wonderopolis: What does a barometer measure?

text: A falling reading on a barometer can mean the weather is about to change. High air pressure usually brings clear skies, and low pressure often brings clouds and rain.

source.name: Wonderopolis: What does a barometer measure?

text: A common rain gauge has a small inner tube that holds exactly one inch of rain. If more rain falls, the extra spills into a bigger tube around it.
On many days a rain gauge reads zero. Weather watchers still write that number down.
Inside a classic thermometer is a thin glass tube of colored liquid. The liquid takes up more room when warm and less room when cool.
A navy officer named Francis Beaufort made a wind scale for ships more than two hundred years ago. It runs from zero to twelve, and people still use it today.
You can judge the wind by watching smoke and leaves. In very calm air, smoke rises straight up.
A cup anemometer has three or four small cups on a spinning stand. The faster the wind blows, the faster the cups spin.

source.name: Met Office: How we measure wind

text: At weather stations, wind tools sit at the top of a mast about ten meters tall. Wind speed is usually given in knots, and one knot is a little more than one mile per hour.

source.name: Met Office: How we measure wind

text: Winds are named for where they blow from. An east wind comes from the east and blows toward the west.

source.name: Met Office: How we measure wind

text: Icicles begin when sunshine melts snow on a roof and the drips freeze at the cold edge. More water runs down, and it freezes at the tip, so the icicle grows longer.
Icicles end in a point. Water runs down them and freezes at the tip, so they get long and thin.
Some frost forms straight from water vapor in the air, without turning into liquid first. It makes tiny ice crystals shaped like scales, needles, or fans.
Frost likes clear, calm nights. Objects near the ground lose heat to the sky and get cold enough to pull water vapor out of the air.
As a snow crystal drifts through a cloud, changes in temperature and dampness change its shape. Some grow into flat plates, and others grow into long needles or stars.
Weather watchers measure snow by pushing a ruler straight down to the ground in several spots. Then they find the average of the readings.

source.name: NWS Roanoke: Measuring snow and sleet

text: A snow board is a flat piece of wood set in an open spot away from trees. After each measurement it is swept clear, so the next reading shows only the new snow.

source.name: NWS Roanoke: Measuring snow and sleet
